title: Rethinking Shift Left In Chip Design
gist: A Semiconductor Engineering roundtable (Synopsys, Silvaco, Axiomise, Hiveware) argues AI agents and digital twins let chip design shift far further left, but trust in surrogate models and agent output is now the gating factor, increasingly closed via formal proofs. Synopsys' Schirrmeister proposes replacing linear shift left with an 'agile', circular refinement model, while others caution requirements and verification bottlenecks remain.

themes.theme: Agentic shift-left and the trust gap

insights.claim: Synopsys' Frank Schirrmeister says compute plus AI agents now allow chip design work to shift much further left than the industry ever expected, but the binding question has become whether early surrogate models are trustworthy representations of the hardware.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Value in EDA is migrating from model generation to model validation and sign-off confidence.
insights.quote: now we have the technical ability with compute, with agents, to shift much further left than we ever hoped we would get to in our lifetimes. The problem there is whether shift left is trustworthy.
insights.locator: There are three changes.

insights.claim: Schirrmeister argues an AI agent cannot be the one to decide whether a surrogate model is accurate; historically a responsible human owned model accuracy in virtual prototyping, and that accountability gap is now open.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop model validation remains a required (and billable) step in agentic flows.
insights.quote: Is the surrogate model a reliable representation of what’s happening? You can’t have the agent decide that.
insights.locator: There are three changes.

insights.claim: If shift-left models are not predictive of final silicon, the early work backfires because teams end up needing another chip spin.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Model predictiveness directly drives respin risk, the largest cost item in advanced-node programs.
insights.quote: Otherwise, you’ll regret you’re shifting left because you’ll need another spin.
insights.locator: There are three changes.

insights.claim: Citing a Qualcomm keynote, Schirrmeister says the industry has moved from a 'productivity gap' to a 'reasoning gap': companies want engineers to reason about and improve products, but tools cannot handle reasoning yet.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: The next EDA battleground is tools that support engineering reasoning, not just throughput.
insights.quote: He said we used to have a productivity gap, but now we have a reasoning gap.
insights.locator: There are three changes.

insights.claim: Once models are trusted, architects could launch 'n' parallel architectural options and evaluate them, turning shift left into rapid design-space exploration.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Trusted models would drive demand for massively parallel compute in early architecture exploration.
insights.quote: At the architectural level, I can decide something and kick off ‘n’ options to try it out if the models are predictive enough.
insights.locator: There are three changes.

insights.claim: Axiomise's Ashish Darbari says shift left has been discussed for at least 15 years; what changed is AI and the agentic use model, and what is still missing is trust in today's AI agents.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Trust tooling, not agent capability, is the gating factor for agentic EDA adoption.
insights.quote: What has changed is AI and the agentic use model. What has not happened yet is the trust element in today’s AI agents.
insights.locator: The shift-left discourse started at least

insights.claim: Silvaco's Jack Berg characterizes AI agents as effectively junior engineers whose work must be reviewed by someone with expertise, rather than replacements for humans.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg
insights.so_what: Agentic AI augments rather than shrinks senior engineering headcount; expertise stays the bottleneck.
insights.quote: The AI agents don’t replace humans. They are effectively junior engineers, and they need to have their work reviewed by somebody who knows it.
insights.locator: That’s a really important point.

insights.claim: Schirrmeister insists teams should not let AI make design decisions or trust it outright, but must drop down to a verified model.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Verified/golden models remain the anchor of value in AI-assisted flows.
insights.quote: You don’t let AI actually make the decision for you, and you don’t trust the AI. You then need to go down into a verified model.
insights.locator: You don’t let AI actually make

themes.theme: Formal verification as the AI trust layer

insights.claim: The top 10 semiconductor companies are adopting agentic AI flows, and Darbari says they are closing the resulting trust gap largely through early adoption of formal verification proofs.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Formal verification vendors are positioned as beneficiaries of agentic AI adoption by large chipmakers.
insights.quote: That trust gap is often being solved through early adoption of formal through proofs.
insights.locator: The shift-left discourse started at least

insights.claim: Some customers are having AI agents rewrite designs, including older-generation ones, for optimized PPA, which raises the problem of proving the rewritten design is equivalent and correct.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: AI-driven design rewriting creates incremental demand for equivalence checking and formal proof.
insights.quote: I know of customers that are taking their designs, even the older generation, and saying, ‘Let an AI agent rewrite it for optimized PPA.’ But how do I know it is correct?
insights.locator: The shift-left discourse started at least

insights.claim: Functional verification is now treated as a top-tier problem on par with security, functional safety, and power, because all of this hardware feeds into the AI ecosystem, which Darbari calls the largest investment pool.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: AI capex is lifting the strategic priority, and budgets, for verification.
insights.quote: functional verification is now seen as a problem, at the same level as security, functional safety, and power
insights.locator: The shift-left discourse started at least

insights.claim: Darbari says the main blocker to formal adoption is not know-how but how seamlessly tools integrate into the overall system.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Integration and workflow fit, not raw capability, will separate winning verification tools.
insights.quote: The know-how is not necessarily the biggest blocker. It’s mostly whether tools can integrate more seamlessly into the system.
insights.locator: The shift-left discourse started at least

insights.claim: Debug time is the real enabler of shift left: failures in architectural analysis can be fed to an agent, but if outputs still require manual review, that review could be a massive blocker in early adoption.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Manual review of agent output may cap productivity gains until insight/triage tooling matures.
insights.quote: if a manual review has to happen, that could be a massive blocker in the early phases of adoption of shift left.
insights.locator: But if you look at what is

insights.claim: Darbari is skeptical that earlier agent adoption alone will yield better designs with fewer bug escapes, saying it remains to be seen and that shift left alone will not fix it.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Do not assume agentic shift left reduces bug escapes; evidence is still pending.
insights.quote: With agents being adopted earlier, will this lead to better designs with fewer bug escapes? That remains to be seen, and I don’t believe that shift left alone will be able to fix it.
insights.locator: But if you look at what is

insights.claim: Many 'spec-to-silicon' efforts assume requirements can be extracted from specification documents, but Darbari notes that most of the time those specs do not exist.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Spec-to-silicon AI pitches face a missing-input problem that limits near-term realism.
insights.quote: people believe you can extract requirements from specification documents — if you have them. But most of the time you don’t have them
insights.locator: The shift-left discourse started at least

insights.claim: Schirrmeister questions whether shift left is even the right model, since it assumes teams can specify six to twelve months ahead what they will build; he proposes setting a general direction and adjusting as information arrives.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Design flows may pivot from waterfall specs to continuous refinement, changing how EDA tools are sold and used.
insights.quote: Shift left assumes that I have a solid knowledge of what I’m actually going to do, and it assumes I can specify what I want six or nine months or a year from now.
insights.locator: Is shift left even the right thing?

insights.claim: Schirrmeister describes an 'agile shift left' where agent-built models let teams decide mid-flow, for example between an Arm processor or a RISC-V processor for a block, and then reset the spec.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Faster architecture what-ifs could make processor IP choices (Arm vs RISC-V) more fluid and later in the cycle.
insights.quote: It’s almost like an agile shift left.
insights.locator: Is shift left even the right thing?

insights.claim: Design used to be sequential, with a product manager committing to a product and finding out 18 months later it didn't work; continuous new data now makes the flow circular and refinable.
insights.speaker: Frank Schirrmeister
insights.so_what: Shorter feedback loops reduce the risk of chips mismatched to workloads by launch.
insights.quote: Now it becomes more circular.
insights.locator: Exactly, and we didn’t dare do this

insights.claim: Darbari pushes back that requirements are not that fuzzy: builders of ML chips, GPUs or CPUs know the derivative design and general architecture; the novel unknowns are implementation choices for power, functionality and AI training or inference.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: Uncertainty is concentrated in implementation, not architecture, so agility has limited scope.
insights.quote: I do not see that things are so fuzzy.
insights.locator: I agree that there are lots of choices

insights.claim: Berg warns that inverse design built from multi-physics solvers, surrogate models and digital twins can return an empty set when constraints are over-specified, which is why design flows must be agile.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg
insights.so_what: Constraint-driven generative design needs iterative relaxation loops, not one-shot specs.
insights.quote: And all of a sudden you have an empty set. It’s over-constrained. Now what do you do?
insights.locator: That’s a really important point.

insights.claim: Hiveware's Ronen Laviv says removing bottlenecks in formal, simulation, and virtual prototyping lets emulation and FPGA prototyping start sooner in the verification pipeline, shifting the whole flow left.
insights.speaker: Ronen Laviv
insights.so_what: Bottleneck relief upstream pulls forward demand for emulation and FPGA prototyping capacity.
insights.quote: then emulation and FPGA can run sooner in the pipeline of doing the verification stuff, and the same thing with simulation.
insights.locator: If we take the example of the

insights.claim: Laviv defines shift left as finding the industry's bottlenecks and pulling work earlier, noting that agents help but also create new bottlenecks or expose old ones.
insights.speaker: Ronen Laviv
insights.so_what: Each agentic speed-up relocates rather than removes the constraint in the flow.
insights.quote: the agents are leaping forward to help, but everything that happens gets us into bottlenecks — new bottlenecks or old bottlenecks — that we have to solve.
insights.locator: Shift left is identifying the bottlenecks

themes.theme: Digital twins and multi-physics down to CFET

insights.claim: Digital twins are being added at the very start of the flow, and Berg says the key challenge is assembling surrogate models from multi-physics data, which requires going back to materials-science and physics solvers for new materials.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg
insights.so_what: TCAD and physics-solver vendors gain relevance as designs move into new materials.
insights.quote: the issue now is working with multi-physics models. Using that data to assemble surrogate models is important.
insights.locator: That’s correct.

insights.claim: Multi-physics surrogate modeling, traditionally outside digital design, is starting to be used for digital design as the industry moves down to the CFET level.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg
insights.so_what: CFET transitions pull TCAD-style physics modeling into mainstream digital design flows.
insights.quote: as we get down to the CFET level, it’s starting to be used there, as well.
insights.locator: That’s correct.

insights.claim: Darbari reports customers going back to the drawing board to build ground-up architectures that can serve different phases of chip use, because training, inference, and power concerns now reach all the way back to the architecture level and software is very different from 20 years ago.
insights.speaker: Ashish Darbari
insights.so_what: AI workloads are forcing clean-sheet architectures, raising validation scope and spend.
insights.quote: who literally are going back to the drawing board to build a ground-up architecture that can address different phases of their chips being used.
insights.locator: The validation problem is significant.
